articles.title: Meet Daisy Campanella, 29, who left Florida behind after inheriting her great-grandmother’s 230-acre Missouri farm, plans to restore neglected land, build family homes and raise animals with husband Philip
articles.summary: Daisy Campanella has traded her life in Florida for a new chapter in rural Missouri after inheriting her great-grandmother’s 230-acre family farm.
articles.body: Daisy Campanella has traded her life in Florida for a new chapter in rural Missouri after inheriting her great-grandmother’s 230-acre family farm. The 29-year-old and her husband, Philip, packed up their belongings, took their two dogs and drove 16 hours to the property, hoping to restore the neglected land, build homes for their family and eventually establish a working farm.Sharing her journey in a video, Daisy spoke about the property’s history, the challenges of starting over and her vision of creating a multi-generational homestead. The farm, once a working dairy operation, now has overgrown pastures, abandoned machinery, vintage vehicles and decades-old belongings waiting to be sorted through.Daisy Campanella plans to restore her great-grandmother’s neglected farmThe property originally belonged to Daisy’s great-grandmother before being passed down to her uncle and eventually inherited by Daisy. According to her, it was once a busy dairy farm, but years of neglect have left parts of the land overgrown. Some areas have reportedly not been properly maintained for around 30 years.“This place needs a lot of work, it needs a lot of work,” Daisy admitted.The farm contains old tractors, vintage vehicles, equipment and containers filled with belongings. Despite the scale of the restoration, Daisy sees the project as an opportunity to preserve her family’s history.“It's not just land. There's an entire family history here,” she said.She hopes to document the transformation and look back in a few years to see how much progress the family has made.Abandoned tractors and vintage vehicles await restorationDaisy estimates that the property contains around 10 to 15 tractors, along with vintage cars and trucks. Some vehicles have remained outdoors for so long that vegetation has grown around them.The couple have already started cleaning up parts of the property, including a vintage Chevrolet truck and a 1982 Ford F-100. They are also sorting through scrap metal, furniture, decorations and other belongings to determine what can be salvaged and what needs to be removed.Clearing overgrown areas and preparing the land for future use will take considerable effort. Daisy understands that the project cannot be completed overnight.“But I try to remind myself that we don't have to do everything overnight,” she said. “This is going to be a project that takes years.”Daisy and Philip are building a house for her grandmotherOne of the couple’s priorities is building a home for Daisy’s grandmother as part of their plan to create a multi-generational homestead. The family is working through the construction process, with the house gradually taking shape.“Watching a house go up from scratch is a completely different experience than just walking into one that's already finished,” Daisy said.Once the house is ready, Daisy and Philip may live there temporarily with her parents while continuing to restore the property. They eventually hope to build additional homes for relatives, allowing family members to live close to one another while maintaining their own spaces.Their long-term vision includes gardens, landscaped areas and a shared space where relatives can gather for meals and celebrations.“It's honestly pretty crazy thinking about what this area could look like in five or 10 years,” she said.Daisy Campanella plans to raise livestock and produce foodThe couple also want to turn the inherited land into a productive farm. Their ideas include raising pasture-raised chickens, cattle and pigs, while researching rotational grazing and other livestock-management practices.“We've been doing a lot of research into pasture-raised chickens, cattle, pigs, and different ways of managing livestock,” Daisy said.According to her, the property has approximately 120 to 130 acres of usable pasture, alongside wooded areas. The couple hope to prepare the land and explore how it can best support their future farming plans.“One of the things I really love about having this much land is that we have room to explore different ideas,” she said.Daisy is particularly interested in understanding where her family’s food comes from and being involved in the process of producing it.“I really love the idea of knowing where our food's coming from,” she explained. “Not just buying something at the grocery store and hoping it's good quality, but actually being involved in the process of raising animals, caring for the land, and producing food.”She also wants to share the difficulties and lessons involved in building a farm from scratch, rather than showing only the finished results.“I want this channel to show the real process, not just the pretty finished result,” she said.Daisy admits leaving Florida has been difficultDespite the excitement of starting over, Daisy acknowledged that moving to rural Missouri has brought challenges. The couple are living in an RV on the property while juggling restoration work, construction and plans for the farm.She also misses being closer to her extended family.“One thing I miss the most is being around the rest of my family,” she said.The scale of the work can sometimes feel overwhelming, especially when the property needs so much attention.“Sometimes I look around and think, what did we get ourselves into?” she admitted.Nevertheless, Daisy believes the long-term goal makes the sacrifices worthwhile. She hopes the farm will eventually become a place where relatives can spend time together, enjoy the outdoors and build memories across generations.Daisy hopes to preserve her family’s legacyFor Daisy, restoring the property is about more than renovating land. She wants to preserve her family’s history while giving the farm a new purpose. Completing her grandmother’s house, clearing overgrown areas and planning the agricultural side of the project remain the immediate priorities.The couple’s broader vision includes additional family homes and livestock operations, although Daisy recognises that transforming the property will take years.“Sometimes I still can't believe this is our life now,” she said, reflecting on the move from Florida to Missouri.She hopes sharing the journey will encourage others to pursue ambitious projects, even when they do not have all the necessary skills at the beginning.“Because if there's one thing I've learned, it's that you don't have to know how to do everything before you start,” Daisy said. “Sometimes you just have to be willing to learn along the way.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Pope says 'there is no such thing as a holy war' in message to religious leaders
articles.summary: The American pope denounced the “troubling revival of war as an instrument of international politics” and its religious justifications by leaders.
articles.body: ROME — Pope Leo XIV denounced any religious justification for wars raging around the world on Tuesday, saying, “There is no such thing as a holy war.” “Only peace is holy,” Leo said in a video message to a gathering of religious leaders in the Italian hilltop town of Assisi. The American pope was supposed to have presided over the gathering in person but had to cancel his participation as he recovers from Oct. 13 lung cancer surgery. Instead, Leo sent a videotaped message that was broadcast to the delegates, who included Archbishop of Canterbury Sarah Mullally, spiritual leader of the worldwide Anglican Communion, as well as Muslim, Buddhist and other Christian leaders. They were in Assisi, the birthplace of the peace-loving St. Francis, to mark the 40th anniversary of a landmark interfaith peace meeting called by St. John Paul II. That encounter, controversial at the time because it featured leaders of different faiths praying together, spawned a movement of interreligious peace appeals and gatherings. In his message, the American pope denounced the “troubling revival of war as an instrument of international politics” and its religious justifications by leaders. “Precisely in these times marked by a culture of power, there is a need to cultivate the spirit of Assisi,” he said. “War can never be waged in the name of God,” he said. “We must rebuild peace everywhere, not prepare for more wars.” Leaders use religion to justify war Russia’s Orthodox Church has justified Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as a “holy war” against a Western world it considers has fallen into evil. Leaders on all sides of the Iran war have used religion to justify their actions. U.S. officials, especially Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, have invoked their Christian faith to cast the war as a Christian nation trying to vanquish its foes with military might. Leo has consistently rejected such justifications as a perversion of religion itself, most stridently in his first encyclical, “Magnificent Humanity,” in which he said fighting in the name of religion “means attacking religion itself.” Vatican brings new aid to Ukraine The Assisi gathering came as the Vatican is accelerating its humanitarian efforts for Ukraine following the entry into effect of a localized ceasefire in the devastated southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky. The pope’s chief almsgiver, Monsignor Luis Marín de San Martín, on Tuesday began a three-day visit to Ukraine and was bringing several trucks’ worth of winter clothes, blankets and food to Kyiv for distribution. Marín de San Martín was planning to visit Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro and Fastiv, Vatican News said. Leo had called for a ceasefire and the delivery of food and medicine in Oleshky, and the safe and voluntary evacuation of its people during an Oct. 16 phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, which the pontiff initiated from the hospital where he was recovering from surgery. Leo followed up three days later, back at the Vatican, with a call to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. According to the Vatican, Leo noted his appeal for a ceasefire to Putin and “expressed the hope that cooperation between both parties will allow for the delivery of food and medical aid, and for the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population.” The White House said the ceasefire in Oleshky was secured by first lady Melania Trump. Asked Tuesday, the Vatican foreign minister, Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, said the Vatican wasn't aware of the first lady's role but also dismissed any polemics over who was ultimately responsible. “I think it’s one of those situations in which it doesn’t matter who actually brought it about or who takes the credit. It’s the fact that hopefully it is real, it will last, it will allow for evacuation and it will allow the arrival of humanitarian aid to help the people who are left behind.” The Vatican initiatives took place after Italian Cardinal Matteo Zuppi, the papal envoy for the Ukraine-Russia war, finished his third mission to Moscow on Sept. 30 and the first under Leo’s pontificate. Zuppi has focused his initiatives on humanitarian issues, especially reuniting Ukrainian children taken by Russia with their families, and Gallagher said for now neither Russia nor Ukraine wants the Holy See to take on a greater mediation or facilitation role.

articles.title: Country star Terri Clark says her band thinks she needs therapy for her fishing addiction
articles.summary: Terri Clark reveals her fishing obsession includes practicing knots on her tour bus ahead of the Champions Celebrity Pro-Am on Old Hickory Lake.
articles.body: Terri Clark has a problem. At least, that's what her band thinks. The country music legend loves fishing so much that she's taken to practicing fishing knots on her tour bus. And apparently, her bandmates have some thoughts. "My band is just like, 'You can get therapy for this. There's a problem,'" Clark joked during an exclusive interview with OutKick OutDoors. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS She blames Instagram. Every time she opens the app, the algorithm feeds her another video promising to teach her the strongest fishing knot known to mankind. Naturally, she has to try it. But if Clark's fishing obsession requires professional intervention, she's about to find herself in excellent company. On Sunday, the Grand Ole Opry member will participate in The Champions Celebrity Pro-Am on Old Hickory Lake near Nashville, where she'll share a boat with one of the world's top professional bass anglers. The Pro-Am follows a three-day championship that brings together 60 of the sport's best anglers competing for a $3.25 million purse. And Clark, who has spent years honing her skills on Lake Erie, can't wait to see how her own fishing knowledge stacks up. "Everybody thinks I'm such a great fisherwoman," she said. "I'm like, they have no idea the level that these guys operate at. I mean, they're professionals. They make a living doing this." Watch Terri Clark's whole interview with OutKick OutDoors here: The difference, she explained, is that she has the luxury of knowing her home waters. Professional anglers, on the other hand, have to figure out unfamiliar lakes, study underwater topography and adapt to whatever conditions they encounter. "I'm going to be taking a master class in bass fishing, which will be super fun." Clark is particularly interested in learning more about fishing electronics. She owns a Humminbird MEGA Live 2 system but hasn't installed it on her boat because, as she put it, she doesn't want to spend all day staring at a camera. Still, she recognizes how useful the technology can be. And if Sunday's fishing lesson happens to reveal a few productive spots on Old Hickory Lake, she certainly won't complain. "I live in Nashville, so maybe I need to mark all the spots we go to so I can go back to them with my kayak later," she joked. The one that got away... for now While Clark is looking forward to learning from the bass fishing pros, there's another fish occupying an awful lot of space in her brain these days. A musky. Preferably one measuring more than 50 inches. She recently returned from a fall fishing trip to Lake Erie, where she'd hoped to finally land one of the elusive predators. Unfortunately, Mother Nature wasn't particularly cooperative. Strong easterly winds kept her off the water for much of the trip, while warmer-than-usual lake temperatures appeared to have delayed the muskies' typical fall movements. But Clark isn't about to admit defeat: "I'm gonna get one though. I'm gonna get one." She's even considering chasing muskies on Tennessee's Caney Fork River, closer to home. In the meantime, she's got plenty of other fish to keep her busy. Lake Erie's multi-species fishing is one of the things she loves most about the lake. On any given day, she might find herself catching bass, northern pike or walleye — sometimes on the same lure. And she has some pretty impressive catches to her name. In 2022, she landed a 16-pound northern pike, a fish so memorable that she had a replica made for her wall after releasing it. But one of her favorite recent fishing memories belongs to somebody else. Over the summer, Clark took comedian Kathleen Madigan out on Lake Erie, where Madigan landed her personal-best bass: a five-and-a-half-pounder. "The fish was bigger than Kathleen," Clark laughed. And watching her friend's excitement was every bit as satisfying as catching a giant fish herself. "When they get something big and they get excited, it's just as exciting as if I caught it myself." Conveniently enough, Madigan will also be competing in Sunday’s Pro-Am. PARKER MCCOLLUM WANTS HIS SONS TO LEARN THE LESSON HUNTING AND RANCH LIFE TAUGHT HIM GROWING UP Not your average relaxing hobby For someone who describes fishing as a meditative experience, Clark has a pretty intense approach to it. "I will dehydrate myself because I won't even stop casting long enough to take a drink of water," she admitted. "I'm so zoned in on it." She's had pike launch themselves out of the water to grab a lure right beside her boat. She's cut her hands badly enough to need bandages while fishing. And she's developed enough knowledge of Lake Erie that she keeps several weather apps handy to make sure it's safe to head out. Even when she's touring, the fishing bug follows her. On days off, she'll hire a guide or find someone willing to take her out on a nearby lake. She generally avoids fishing on show days, though, because the possibility of a boat breakdown causing her to miss soundcheck isn't a risk she's willing to take. But it's not just the thrill of landing a big fish that keeps her coming back. "It's not just about catching fish. It's not just about fishing," she said. "It's about being surrounded by nature." SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER After more than three decades in a career that involves bright lights, loud crowds and constant travel, Clark finds something entirely different on the water. She described watching the sunrise over Lake Erie at 6:30 in the morning, with the water perfectly still, and being so overwhelmed by the beauty of the moment that she's been moved to tears. "It's almost like you're part of nature's heartbeat at that time, and I don't know a better way of putting it." That's also an experience she hopes more women and young girls will discover for themselves. "I think that we need more female anglers out there," she said. Her advice for beginners? Don't overcomplicate it. Find someone knowledgeable who can teach you, start with basic equipment and build your skills over time. And don't underestimate the humble wacky rig, which she says still catches bass as reliably as just about anything else. As for Clark, she's still learning, still chasing bigger fish and still looking for the next excuse to get out on the water. Her remaining bucket-list goals include headlining Colorado's iconic Red Rocks Amphitheatre and landing that 50-plus-inch musky. And when asked about those two dreams, Clark made one thing very clear. "Don't ask me though if I had to choose Red Rocks or the musky. Don't ask me which one." articles.title: How will Budget announcement affect Wales, as Plaid demand more cash
articles.summary: Welsh Finance Minister Elin Jones has called for a spending plan that "finally treats us fairly".
articles.body:
Plaid Cymru ministers say they want extra cash for railways and public services in Wales ahead of the UK government's Budget on Wednesday.

Welsh Finance Minister Elin Jones called for the Chancellor John Healey to set out a spending plan that "finally treats us fairly".

The Budget announces Westminster's tax and spending plans for the year ahead - and more cash given to English public services could result in extra spending in Wales where they are devolved.

A UK government spokesperson said the chancellor would focus on giving households and businesses "a bit of breathing space where we can".

Minimum wage set to rise but 18-20 year-olds will not get bigger increase

Healey to shield low-income pensioners from income tax in the Budget

Meanwhile, shoppers in one of Wales' busiest markets told BBC Wales that once again the cost of living was their biggest concern before the spending announcement.

Any extra spending for things in England that are controlled in Wales by the Welsh government - like healthcare, schools and roads - could trigger additional cash for the country.

Elin Jones had asked the chancellor to bring forward £1bn of the £14bn the UK Labour government had promised for long-term rail funding in Wales.

She also asked for extra money to help the Welsh government set its budget for 2027-28, which currently faces a real-term cut in day-to-day spending.

She previously claimed Wednesday's settlement could be the worst for the Welsh government since the Covid-19 pandemic.

Jones said Wales had been short-changed "for years".

"This UK Budget is the moment of truth, and we need the chancellor to act, not just acknowledge the problem," she said.

"Wales pulls its weight in the UK economy. We contribute. Now we need the UK government to match that ambition with action and deliver a budget that finally treats us fairly."

There have also been calls from Labour MP Nia Griffith to give the Welsh government greater flexibility to borrow to fund investment projects.

A senior Welsh Labour source said they had been "pressing really hard for fiscal flexibility", along the lines of Griffith's request.

Ahead of Wednesday's announcement, shoppers and traders at Swansea Market said the cost of living was their biggest concern.

"Will we be able to see through the winter without having to borrow money," said shopper Louise. "It's quite a worry."

Like others at the market, Louise admitted feeling "anxious" about the winter, despite having saved some money with her supplier.

Help with energy costs was the top of many people's lists of things they wanted help with in the Budget.

Prices rose at the beginning of the month and typical bills are forecast to increase by 16% in January because of the conflict in the Middle East .

Dad-of-two Richard said his wage did not keep up with rising energy bills, leaving his family "penny pinching towards the end of the month".

"Things that we used to have as a bit of luxury are out of the question, days out with family cost a fortune," he said.

Rural homes that use heating oil have also seen a dramatic increase in costs. The chancellor had already announced he will remove import taxes to bring the price down a little.

Healey has talked about giving people "breathing space" from cost-of-living pressures, and revealed a package of small measures he is calling "everyday fixes" ahead of the Budget.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham also wants to cut standing charges from gas bills.

If further support is offered in the Budget, it would be likely limited and targeted to the poorest households.

The cost of filling up cars soared this year as the conflict in the Middle East pushed up the price of oil.

Petrol prices hit a four - year high in September , and diesel has also shot up.

The cost of transporting fruit and veg is one issue putting pressure on Gareth Evans, who is the fourth generation of his family to run the Get Fresh stall at Swansea Market.

"It's a struggle at the moment," he said.

"We get costs passed on to us from our suppliers.

"We've also got vans ourselves and we supply caterers and diesel is very expensive."

Emma, who runs a pet store, said her rising costs meant she has had to increase prices for customers, as "it goes down the line".

She believes many working people are "struggling to live now".

The chancellor is expected to freeze the planned increase in fuel duty in January.

The rate was reduced by 5p by the previous Conservative government in 2022 and that measure has already been extended twice.

One of Elin Jones' requests is for the UK government's help for a flagship scheme to help address child poverty.

The Welsh government is planning a trial scheme paying 15,000 children in families on universal credit £10 a week.

The Cynnal scheme is modelled on the Scottish government's child payment which helped to reduce child poverty in Scotland.

Welsh ministers have asked the UK government to exempt the payments from tax and benefits calculations, so recipients do not see a cut to their income.

BBC Wales has been told discussions about the child payment are still ongoing, which suggests there will be no announcement on Wednesday.

Burnham had previously said he was "open" to considering this, and it has already been granted to facilitate the scheme in Scotland.

The chancellor will also announce how much the state pension will increase by next year.

It looks likely to top £13,000 a year with the full, flat rate expected to increase by £488 a year in April due to the triple lock guarantee .

One thing that has already been announced is that pensioners who rely entirely on the state pension will be shielded from paying income tax, which usually kicks in at £12,570.

The specific details will be announced in the Budget.

On working age welfare, Healey has been rolling the pitch to prepare Labour MPs for potential cuts to the benefits bill, with a carefully scripted speech at this year's party conference.

There are reports that young people not in education, work or training may see big changes to their support, but that could be unveiled after the Budget when former Health Secretary Alan Milburn publishes his recommendations for reform.

Reform UK Senedd member Cai Parry Jones said his party "would stop using Welsh people as cash cows", and would build an M4 relief road, scrap family farm tax, and "reward working people" by raising tax-free personal allowance to £15,000.

Welsh Conservative Senedd leader Darren Millar called for the UK government to make money available for major road projects, including an M4 relief road, and more defence spending in Wales, calling for a "pro-union Budget deal".

David Chadwick, Welsh Liberal Democrat MP, said his party wanted a Budget that gave Welsh families "some much-needed breathing space", calling for a 10p cut in fuel duty, a guarantee to bring down energy bills, and a temporary VAT cut for hospitality.

The Budget comes ahead of the first substantive meeting between the prime minister and the first minister at the National Economic Council later this week, where devolution is expected to be discussed.

A UK government spokesperson said: "The chancellor is focused on giving households and businesses a bit of breathing space where we can. That's why we have removed VAT from electricity bills, extended the 5p fuel duty cut and frozen rail fares."

articles.title: No clear mandate projected in Israel election: What’s next?
articles.summary: President Isaac Herzog will task the candidate he deems best placed to form a government once results are in.
articles.body:
Exit polls from Israel’s legislative elections have come in, with no party or bloc projected to secure a clear mandate to form a new government.

The polls, released by the major Israeli television networks on Tuesday, indicated that the coalition led by current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party was on track to win 51 seats in Israel’s 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.

The opposition bloc led by former Israeli military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party was also projected to take 51 seats.

That could leave neither bloc with the 61 seats needed for a majority, setting the stage for weeks or months of political jockeying to form Israel’s next government.

Separately, the Arab-led parties, which are not part of either coalition, were projected to win 18 seats. This means the Arab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers if other parties agree to join forces with them.

Eisenkot said the exit polls show a “lack of confidence” in Netanyahu, while Yair Lapid, the current opposition leader, said the prime minister’s bloc has suffered a “crushing defeat”. He added, “This is a total collapse, and the public has told them to go home.”

But Gideon Saar, Israel’s foreign minister and a member of Netanyahu’s Likud party, said the opposition’s celebrations were premature.

In a social media post, he said: “Likud is the largest party in Israel. It is always good to learn something from the past.”

Netanyahu, who heads Likud, has served as prime minister for nearly 19 of the past 30 years and has repeatedly survived political crises.

Ehab Jabareen, a Palestinian political analyst and researcher in Israel, told Al Jazeera that the early exit poll projections show “a clear weakening of Netanyahu’s bloc” but expressed caution about “declaring either a Netanyahu victory or the end of his political career”.

“The exit polls suggest that his bloc has lost its majority, but they also suggest that his opponents face a difficult task in building one,” he said. “If neither side can form a government, Netanyahu could remain in office as caretaker while the negotiations continue.”

Who will the president nominate to form a government?

Once the final vote tally is in on November 4, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will speak with party leaders about who they want as prime minister, then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.

That will not necessarily be the leader of the party that won the most seats in the Knesset.

With Netanyahu and Eisenkot’s parties emerging as the strongest, the two are viewed as leading contenders.

How much time will the invited leader have to form a coalition?

Up to 42 days. The candidate initially has 28 days, but the president can extend it by 14 days.

During this time, parties could engage in intensive negotiations and dealmaking, seeking policy concessions or potential ministerial portfolios, as the designated candidate tries to cobble together enough support to govern.

If the candidate cannot assemble a coalition with at least 61 seats, they could also try to form a minority government by relying on support from smaller parties, or negotiate a power-sharing arrangement with alternating prime ministers.

To be sworn in, a new government must win a parliamentary confidence vote by a simple majority, which can be fewer than 61 votes if some parties abstain.

If the first candidate fails to form a government, Herzog has the option of asking another Knesset member to try to do so within 28 days. If that candidate also fails, a majority of Knesset members could put forward a third candidate, who would have a final 14 days to try to assemble one.

If the Knesset remains at an impasse, it would be formally dissolved, and Israelis would return to the polls for another round of elections.

Those elections would have to be called within 90 days. In the meantime, Netanyahu’s government would remain in office as a caretaker government.

Prolonged gridlock in the Knesset forced Israelis into three rounds of elections between April 2019 and March 2020. The result was a power-sharing agreement between Netanyahu and his then-chief rival, Benny Gantz, under which they were supposed to rotate the premiership.

That government collapsed a year later after failing to pass a budget.

Will the opposition form a coalition with the Arab-led parties?

While the exit polls suggest the Arab-led parties could become kingmakers, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have ruled out partnering with the parties, citing a lack of shared values.

Asaf Ronel, an Israeli political analyst, said that while exit polls suggest an end to Netanyahu’s “nightmarish government”, there are serious questions if other leaders can overcome their “racism and refusal” to collaborate with the Arab-led groups.

“The question now is whether they can let go of their racist elections promise, otherwise the most likely scenarios is that we are back to another round of elections in the next few months,” he said.

images.caption: Activists of Israel's Yashar party hang a campaign poster featuring party leader Gadi Eisenkot during Israel's general elections, in Herzliya, Israel, on October 27, 2026 [Amir Levy/Getty Images]

articles.title: Flavio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after Lula defeat, US offers visas to family
articles.summary: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has fleed the country for the United States after losing the presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da
articles.body: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has fleed the country for the United States after losing the presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, with the US State Department set to issue entry visas to him and his family, Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing three sources.Bolsonaro’s departure came after he failed to comply with a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports within 24 hours. The court had ordered the passports seized over a money laundering probe, in which Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing, citing concerns that he could flee Brazil and his “significant financial resources”. Two sources told Reuters that his passports were cancelled after the deadline expired.The location of Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters was not immediately clear. A source close to the family told Reuters that he had landed in Florida but declined to specify where. BBC report suggests that Bolsonaro is in Miami.“The State Department will issue visas to Flavio Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the United States,” a senior US State Department official told Reuters.Bolsonaro’s departure could deepen tensions between Washington and Brasil. Lula has accused the US of colluding with the Bolsonaro family to bring them back to power.US president Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed that former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio’s father, was the target of judicial persecution. Trump also said on Monday that Brazil’s election “looked like another rigged election”, without providing evidence in the remarks cited by Reuters.Lula, speaking in Brasilia, said he had just learned of Flavio’s departure and called it shameful, arguing that the senator should have stayed in Brazil to prove his innocence.Flavio Bolsonaro has yet to formally concede defeat. On Sunday, he said he would seek to annul the election result over alleged voter irregularities, although his Liberal Party said on Monday that it acknowledged Lula’s victory.The circumstances of his departure remain unclear. A senior Brazilian federal police official told Reuters that Bolsonaro had not left the country through any regular migration point.On Monday, Bolsonaro had denied any intention of fleeing Brazil, saying he would surrender his passports and defend himself against what he called an attempt to intimidate him. His campaign manager, senator Rogerio Marinho, said he was surprised by reports of the departure, adding that they had discussed Bolsonaro taking on the role of opposition leader after receiving about 60 million votes.Bolsonaro is due to lose his immunity from prosecution when his Senate term ends in February. His departure also echoes that of his father, who went to the United States after refusing to concede defeat to Lula in 2022. Jair Bolsonaro later returned to Brazil and was sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup after his supporters stormed government buildings in Brasilia.You use AI every day. articles.title: 14 years after UNC student’s death, man is convicted of raping and killing her
articles.summary: Faith Hedgepeth was a 19-year-old sophomore when she was beaten to death in her apartment in 2012. Miguel Salguero Olivares, 33, was sentenced to life in prison on the murder charge.
articles.body: A man accused of killing a North Carolina college student 14 years ago was convicted of first-degree murder, rape and other charges after prosecutors told jurors that forensic evidence was “screaming his name.” Faith Hedgepeth was a 19-year-old sophomore at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill when she was beaten to death in her off-campus apartment in September 2012. Miguel Salguero Olivares was arrested nine years later after being pulled over for driving while intoxicated and providing a DNA sample that prosecutors say matched evidence from the crime scene. Salguero Olivares, 33, did not testify during the trial in Durham, and his attorneys rested their case without calling any witnesses. Jurors deliberated for six hours over two days before they convicted him Friday of murder, rape, sexual offense and burglary. He was then sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole on the murder charge plus 45 to 65 years on the other charges. Hedgepeth’s mother, Connie Hedgepeth, told the judge that she forgave her daughter’s killer long ago. “It was just three weeks after her death. It didn’t matter who done it, I knew that I had to forgive, and I do forgive, but my heart aches for his family,” she said. “It was just such a senseless and cruel act, but we have to go on, and we just have to trust God and go on with our lives.” Roland Hedgepeth, Faith’s father, said losing his daughter was like having his heart ripped out. He called her a beacon of hope who was born at a low point in his life and admitted it had been easier over the past 5,158 days to say he forgave someone he didn’t know. “Today it got very real,” he said. “Nevertheless, I say it without reservation, I forgive Miguel for what he did.” Calling those statements “powerful and kind,” defense attorney James Rainsford said he also could speak about his client and his client's family but decided not to. “For me to try to blend the two things, I don't think that's what everybody needs at this point.” Defense argued its client was falsely accused In closing arguments Thursday, defense attorneys accused investigators of having “tunnel vision” in assuming that their client was a monster and not a “19-year-old boy” who had consensual sex with the victim days before her death. Prosecutors, meanwhile, urged jurors to rely on DNA evidence instead of distractions from the defense team. “We know who did it. The forensic evidence is screaming his name,” said prosecutor Angela Garcia-Lamarca, who described the “uncurable agony” Hedgepeth's family has endured. “When the defendant brought that bottle down on her head and she started to bleed, that was the start of a bleeding that still hasn’t stopped,” she said. “He sentenced her to death. He sentenced everybody else who loved her to life. There was no one there to protect her. There was no one there to stop him — until now. Y’all are here. You’re here now, and you can stop him.” Prosecution suggests victim spurned defendant's advances Nearly two dozen witnesses testified for the prosecution, including crime scene technicians, state and local law enforcement, a DNA expert and Hedgepeth's friends. Hedgepeth's roommate, Karena Rosario, testified that she was drunk and sick when Hedgepeth drove them home from a club around 2 a.m. that Sept. 7. She said she later called a friend to pick her up, leaving Hedgepeth in the apartment alone. She returned hours later to find her roommate’s body. Though no witnesses corroborated the theory, prosecutors suggested Salguero Olivares may have attended a barbecue hosted by Hedgepeth’s neighbor that night, unsuccessfully hit on the young women in the parking lot and then returned, embarrassed and angry, after Rosario left. Forensic evidence was a focus Experts testified that the defendant’s fingerprints and palm print were found on a wine bottle at the scene and that his DNA was found in Hedgepeth’s body, on a note written on a fast-food bag found at the scene and on a rum bottle covered in blood that investigators identified as the weapon in the killing. Defense attorneys questioned Rosario’s account of that night, the processing of the crime scene and the reliability of some DNA evidence. They pointed out that police failed to search some areas of the apartment and later lost some possible blood evidence and emphasized that DNA from sexual intercourse can remain for days afterward. “Maybe he was living the same life as other 19- and 20-year-old children that we’ve heard about in this case,” defense attorney Jason Murphy said. “Maybe he had too much to drink, maybe he forgot about an encounter.” But special prosecutor Lisa Coltrane dismissed that as “noise.” “No matter what kind of mistakes were made or things that were missed, it doesn’t erase the palm print; it doesn’t somehow lift the DNA out of Faith,” she said. “They didn’t talk to every single person in Chapel Hill, and it doesn’t matter. They still got the guy because he left his DNA like confetti all over that room.”

articles.title: Travelers may face major disruptions as strikes threaten airports and popular attractions
articles.summary: Rail strikes may hit Spain's Renfe and Ouigo train services on Thursday and Friday, while Italy's general strike is threatening trains, flights and ground travel.
articles.body: Travelers heading to Italy and Spain could face major transportation disruptions this week as workers prepare to strike. Rail passengers in Spain could see delays and cancellations beginning Thursday, Oct. 29, while a nationwide strike in Italy on Friday could affect trains, flights and other forms of transportation, according to reports. In Spain, train drivers represented by the SEMAF union are planning a 24-hour strike Thursday that will affect Renfe, Spain's national passenger rail company, according to an announcement from the union. US WARNS AMERICANS TO STAY VIGILANT AS TERROR RISK LOOMS AT MAJOR VACATION HOT SPOT SEMAF cited concerns, including railway safety, working conditions and what it described as unfulfilled commitments as reasons for the strike. The strike is scheduled to run from 12:01 a.m. through 11:59 p.m., the union said. Some trains will continue operating during the strike under minimum service requirements. The Spanish government has required 73% of Renfe's high-speed and long-distance trains and 65% of its medium-distance trains to run during the strike, according to Renfe. Renfe has pushed back against some of the reasons given for the strike. The company said it's completed the steps it was responsible for under a February agreement aimed at improving the country's rail system, according to a company press release. FURIOUS CROWDS PROTEST SKY-HIGH HOUSING COSTS AND MASS TOURISM IN MAJOR CITY It also said it has moved forward with additional hiring and taken steps to improve train maintenance, while arguing that several other issues raised by the union are controlled by government agencies or other organizations. "Is it safe to travel or should I reschedule the trip?" "Renfe respects the exercise of the right to strike but regrets a call that could affect thousands of travelers despite the progress made and full compliance with the obligations assumed by the company in the February agreement," the company said in a translated press release. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Travel problems in Spain could continue Friday, when drivers for Ouigo, another high-speed rail operator, are planning a separate 24-hour strike over working conditions, according to Business Travel News Europe. Meanwhile, travelers in Italy could face disruptions to several forms of transportation. A nationwide general strike is scheduled for Friday, Oct. 30, with transportation workers among those expected to take part, according to Italy's Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport. Rail workers are scheduled to strike from 9 p.m. Thursday through 8:59 p.m. Friday, according to the ministry's strike calendar. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Air travel could also face disruptions Friday, while ground-handling workers at Florence and Pisa airports are planning a separate 24-hour strike, according to the government schedule. Reasons for the strike include concerns over the cost of living, wages and pensions, as well as opposition to increased military spending, according to the USB union. The strike comes amid broader unrest in Italy, where recent demonstrations have led to clashes and prompted the government to deploy additional soldiers to Milan, Fox News Digital previously reported. The upcoming strikes have already left some tourists questioning whether they should change their plans. Some commenters urged other travelers to check whether their specific train is included on a guaranteed service list before making any changes. "There is nothing unsafe about a transportation strike," one person wrote, adding that travelers should check their train before deciding whether to reschedule. Other travelers said they would rather avoid the uncertainty altogether. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I would reschedule if you can," one Reddit user wrote. articles.title: Need to balance right to free speech, privacy: Supreme Court
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: SC on Tuesday acknowledged the importance of media’s right to freedom of speech and expression but said this needed to be balanced with
articles.body: NEW DELHI: SC on Tuesday acknowledged the importance of media’s right to freedom of speech and expression but said this needed to be balanced with citizens’ right to privacy and dignity and asked petitioner Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) to suggest how these two rights could coexist harmoniously.Entertaining DNPA’s petition terming certain provisions of Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the amendment to RTI Act redefining ‘personal information’ as an attempt towards pre-censorship of news content that violated the media’s right to free speech and impeded media independence, SC said, “You are domain experts. You suggest to the govt and SC how to harmonise the two competing rights.Privacy act will hit freedom of Press: Digital news bodyA bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymlaya Bagchi and V Mohana said: “Media must ensure there is no misuse of the rights enjoyed by it. There must be a balance between your rights and the rights of innocent citizens. We will have to leave it to you to suggest how best you are going to ensure that the media’s rights are not misused and the right to privacy of citizens are not violated.”Appearing for the petitioner, senior advocate Madhavi Divan said provisions of DPDP Act failed to provide exemption in favour of journalistic activity as a distinct class and had brought the regime of notice and prior consent within it, which would lead to closure of newsrooms as they feed live information. If journalists went around seeking consent of people, then no news could be disseminated, she said.“It is not merely the fundamental right to speech and expression and dissemination of information owing to freedom of the press which has been set at nought by the aforesaid provision, but the DPDP Act places myriad restrictions in the manner in which information is accessed, processed and disseminated,” DNPA said.“In the absence of exemptions, the entire scheme under Chapter II of DPDP Act will constitute unreasonable restrictions upon journalists in the exercise of the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression and practise any profession or to carry on any occupation, trade or business,” it added.The petitioner complained that DPDP Act imposed onerous conditions governing how information was to be disseminated and how access was obtained and cited an SC judgement, which had ruled that the fundamental right to know could not be sacrificed at the altar of privacy.The bench issued notice to the Centre on the petition and tagged it with a clutch of petitions which are scheduled for hearing on Nov 17.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Arunachal Pradesh: A border official's remarks cast a shadow over India-China thaw
articles.summary: India-China ties were on a cautious recovery path until a border official’s remarks raised fresh doubts about ground realities.
articles.body:
For much of the past year, India-China relations appeared to be on a cautious path to recovery.

The two countries have seen ups and downs in their ties over decades - especially over the disputed Himalayan frontier.

But events of the past few days suggest that the thaw which has followed their most recent clashes in 2020 may be more fragile than it seems.

The latest concerns began when India's border police chief said Chinese troops had returned to disputed areas along the Himalayan frontier in large numbers earlier this year, pitching tents several kilometres inside territory claimed by India.

The remarks by Shatrujeet Singh Kapur, director general of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), have triggered a political controversy in Delhi.

To begin with, such comments by serving officials are rare. Sensitive border issues are usually addressed by the federal government through its defence or foreign ministries.

At a recent gathering of officers in Rajasthan state, Kapur said face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops had taken place at several locations in the north-eastern state of Arunachal Pradesh and were continuing.

The confrontations began in July, he said, but both sides initially withdrew.

A few days later, Chinese troops returned in larger numbers and pitched tents "around six-to-seven kilometres inside India's perception of the Line of Actual Control (LAC)", he added.

The LAC is an ill-defined line separating the areas controlled by the neighbours and India and China have sparred for decades over this disputed 3,440km (2,100-mile) border.

China claims Arunachal Pradesh as part of southern Tibet. But Delhi has always rejected the claim, saying the state was an integral part of India.

The dispute is one of the most persistent challenges inherited by independent India from the British colonial rule in 1947. It led to a brief border war in 1962, in which India suffered a humiliating defeat.

More than six decades later, much of the frontier remains undemarcated, with the two countries maintaining overlapping territorial claims.

The region's rugged terrain adds to the challenge: shifting river courses, lakes and snow-covered peaks make it difficult to establish a clear boundary.

As a result, troops from the two sides can find themselves face-to-face along the frontier, sometimes triggering violent clashes and diplomatic tensions.

The last major escalation came in June 2020 , when Indian and Chinese troops clashed in the Galwan Valley in Ladakh. At least 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese soldiers were killed.

It was the first fatal confrontation between the two sides since 1975. Indian opposition parties accused the government of losing territory to China - a claim Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government has repeatedly rejected.

The clashes triggered a sharp deterioration in relations, disrupting diplomatic engagement and affecting trade and travel. After several rounds of negotiations, the neighbours agreed in 2024 to take steps towards easing border tensions.

They have since moved to restore direct flights and ease visa restrictions imposed after the clashes.

Chinese President Xi Jinping also visited India in September for the Brics summit, his first visit to the country in seven years.

These developments raised hopes of a broader normalisation of ties. But the latest reported stand-offs have renewed questions about how much progress has actually been made on the ground.

After Kapur's comments, the main opposition Congress party once again accused Modi of making concessions to Beijing.

"The prime minister and his entire apparatus remain silent on this grave issue," senior Congress leader Jairam Ramesh wrote on X .

The Indian government has not explicitly denied Kapur's account that Chinese troops had pitched tents several kilometres inside what India considers to be its side of the LAC.

Foreign ministry spokesman Randhir Jaiswal said last week that "the situation in the border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns".

He said both countries were using military and diplomatic channels to address outstanding issues, but gave no further details.

A Chinese foreign ministry spokesman said that China had "consistently and strictly adhered to relevant agreements" reached with India and it conducted "normal patrol and management activities in the border areas to safeguard territorial sovereignty".

Experts say Kapur's remarks offer a rare glimpse into what they describe as China's increasingly assertive military posture along the disputed frontier.

"This pattern of Chinese probing at various points of the Arunachal Pradesh border has been happening for some time," Shyam Saran, a former Indian foreign secretary who led several rounds of border talks with China in the mid-2000s, told the BBC.

He said such actions were "not enough to result in an immediate war, but enough to sort of create new facts on the ground".

Indian opposition parties have long accused China of extending its presence in both Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh, leading to tensions.

Zhou Bo, a retired senior colonel in China's People's Liberation Army who is now associated with Tsinghua University in Beijing, said both countries had learnt lessons from the 2020 Galwan clashes.

"The two sides should be more careful to avoid this kind of thing from happening in the future," he said, adding that Chinese media had not reported on the latest stand-offs in Arunachal Pradesh.

India and China's tensions also come against the backdrop of a complicated economic relationship.

Despite their differences, the countries remain major trading partners, with bilateral trade reaching $151bn last year. But the balance is heavily tilted in Beijing's favour, with Chinese exports to India accounting for about $131bn.

India continues to rely on Chinese imports for machinery, rare earth magnets, electric vehicle batteries and pharmaceutical products.

This dependence means tensions with Beijing can have consequences well beyond the border, particularly for Indian industries and infrastructure projects.

Last week, China also announced restrictions on exports of tunnel-boring machines used in metro rail and highway construction, saying they were intended to protect national security and national interests. Although these curbs were not India specific, they would have a bearing on India's infrastructure push.

"Chinese policy towards India is designed to complicate India's rise, including India's ability to master certain things in advanced technology and manufacturing," Christopher Clary, a professor at the University at Albany in New York, told the BBC.

A similar problem emerged last year when China restricted export of rare earth magnets - widely used in electric vehicles, smartphones, wind turbines and medical scanners.

The move temporarily caused supply problems for Indian industries, highlighting how Beijing's control over key materials can affect global supply chains.

India is now trying to build domestic capacity to produce rare earth magnets, but developing the industry will take time and investment.

For people living along the disputed frontier, the consequences of tensions with China are more immediate.

"Villagers living in some border areas tell us that they cannot access grazing lands because of Chinese intrusion and encroachment. It's not something new, it's been happening for a long time," says Tongam Rina, a senior journalist with the Arunachal Times.

This has created a "sense of insecurity among the people here," she adds.

Villagers usually do not return to those "prohibited" areas for hunting and yak rearing, and they are not sure when they would be allowed again.

The border dispute also has wider strategic implications for Delhi, with a growing realisation that President Donald Trump's focus on expanding economic engagement with China could limit Washington's willingness to back India in any future confrontation with Beijing.

China may have little interest in a full-scale conflict with India but, analysts say, it could see advantages in allowing the dispute to continue.

As China's economic and military power grows, it may calculate that a prolonged stalemate will strengthen its position in any future negotiations.

For India, the latest stand-offs are a reminder that improved diplomatic ties do not necessarily translate into lasting stability along the border.

articles.title: Netanyahu, Eisenkot camps clash over Israeli election projections
articles.summary: Despite narrower exit poll figures, opposition leaders insisted the result was a defeat for the government.
articles.body:
Israeli political leaders have traded sharp reactions to exit poll projections showing no clear winner between the country’s main political blocs.

Updated figures broadcast by Israel’s Channel 13 showed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud-led coalition tied at 51 seats with the opposition bloc led by challenger Gadi Eisenkot in the 120-seat Knesset.

Despite narrower exit poll figures, opposition leaders insisted the result was a defeat for the government.

Eisenkot, head of the Yashar party and a former military chief of staff, told supporters after voting closed that the initial projections showed a “complete lack of confidence in Netanyahu and the October 7 government”, according to the AFP news agency.

“Don’t let anyone confuse you: the Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat,” opposition leader Yair Lapid said in a statement. “This is a total collapse and the public has told them to go home.”

Under the updated figures, unaligned Arab parties were expected to hold 18 seats, leaving both major camps 10 seats short of the 61 required for an absolute majority.

Supporters at Eisenkot’s watch party in Tel Aviv cheered projections as voter turnout reached 77.7 percent, according to the Central Elections Committee.

However, senior figures in Netanyahu’s camp pushed back against opposition declarations, saying the final results could shift the balance.

Gideon Saar, Israel’s foreign minister and a key Netanyahu ally, dismissed opposition statements as “premature”, writing on social media that Likud remained the largest single party in parliament.

Meanwhile, leaders of Arab political factions highlighted their potential role in upcoming coalition negotiations.

“We will transform the mandate we received into a new reality in the country,” Mansour Abbas, leader of the United Arab List (Ra’am), told reporters.

At the Joint List alliance headquarters in Nazareth, candidate Faten Gattas told supporters that high participation among Palestinian citizens of Israel aimed to block the return of Netanyahu’s nationalist coalition.

“We refuse the occupation and racism, and we will remain here,” Gattas said, according to the Reuters news agency.

With neither camp reaching a governing majority, political analysts suggested smaller parties would be key deciders as formal coalition talks begin in the coming days.

articles.title: Arab parties projected to win 18 seats in Israeli parliamentary election
articles.summary: Record-breaking voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel hits around 80 percent, early indications show.
articles.body:
Israel’s Arab parties are projected to win 18 seats in the Israeli parliament, exit polls indicate, after voting among Palestinian citizens of Israel surged to their highest levels in decades.

Exit polling data from Tuesday’s vote suggested that the leading Arab-led parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, are set to hold a record number of seats in the 120-member Knesset. Updated exit polling indicated that the opposition bloc led by former Israeli military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party and the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party were tied at 51 seats each.

Early indications put voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel at around 80 percent, historic numbers that break 1999 records, Israel’s Channel 12 reported on Tuesday.

The leader of Ra’am, or the United Arab List, Mansour Abbas, said he hopes the final election results will allow the anti-Netanyahu bloc, including his party, to win the 61 seats required to form a government.

“With the numbers we have now, there is no government,” Abbas told Israel’s Channel 12.

Abbas, whose Ra’am party currently holds five seats in the Knesset and joined the coalition that governed Israel from 2021 to 2022, added that both main blocs reached out to his party before and after the election.

Speaking to Al Jazeera, Alon Pinkas, a former Israeli ambassador, said creating a government might prove difficult for parties such as Eisenkot’s – which earlier exit polls had put narrowly ahead – because they promised not to form coalitions with Arab parties during the campaign.

“There’s a price to pay,” Pinkas said, because the “Arabs can’t be kept outside and only being considered and co-opted when you need their votes”.

He added that the Arab-led lists will make demands that a Jewish-led coalition government may not support.

Netanyahu and his far-right coalition made last-ditch efforts on Tuesday to get their supporters to the polls, warning of surging voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel , a tactic Arab politicians denounced as racist and inflammatory .

Cars flying Netanyahu’s Likud party flags drove through Jerusalem blaring the Islamic call to prayer and urging supporters to cast their ballots because “Arabs are voting”, witnesses said.

In social media posts, the embattled prime minister highlighted long queues at polling stations in Arab communities and published an image that he said showed Arab voters, including women wearing the niqab, a veil that covers the lower half of the face, waiting to vote.

“If we don’t wake up now, we’ll find ourselves with a government of Mansour Abbas and Ahmad Tibi,” he said, referring to two leading Palestinian members of the Knesset.

Overall voter turnout was also historic, reaching its highest level since 1999 with 77.7 percent casting ballots in Tuesday’s election, the Central Elections Committee reported. Palestinian citizens of Israel make up about 21 percent of the country’s population of 10 million and have traditionally voted at lower rates than Jewish Israelis.

Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, called the election “an existential moment for Palestinian-Israelis”.

She noted the record turnout among what has emerged as a key voting bloc, which drew “even [voters] who would usually boycott elections, who didn’t believe it would amount to any kind of influence, that it would change their reality, that it would alter the systemic discrimination that they face”.

The Knesset has passed more than 100 laws discriminating against Palestinian citizens of Israel, who also face discrimination in receiving state funds, Odeh said.

articles.title: Israelis shatter turnout records to pass wartime judgement on Bibi
articles.summary: Israelis surged to the polls Tuesday at a pace that shattered records, to pass wartime judgment on PM Benjamin Netanyahu in what voters described as the
articles.body: Israelis surged to the polls Tuesday at a pace that shattered records, to pass wartime judgment on PM Benjamin Netanyahu in what voters described as the most consequential election in the nation’s history. Long queues formed outside polling stations for the first election since the Oct 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks, with voters engaged over the trauma of the country’s deadliest day and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.The Central Elections Committee reported that 66.7% of eligible voters had already cast their ballots within the first nine hours of voting, a record by that point in the day with six more hours to go.Policies of Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition have been divisive at home and have deepened Israel’s international isolation, while he has defended his record, calling himself the only leader with the mettle to face down Israel’s foes. Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader with 19 years in office, is an unmatched political survivor, and his nationalist politics are increasingly entrenched. Israel’s fragmented system makes it difficult for an array of opponents to force out his coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.His main rival Gadi Eisenkot, a military ex-chief of staff and security hawk, aims to unseat him with the support of parties on the right and centre, as well as the rump of an increasingly marginalised left. Opinion polls show a close race.In a message to supporters, Netanyahu urged them to vote, saying turnout was high among his opponents on the left and among Israelis of Arab heritage, around a fifth of the country. “We need it to be high too. You all need to stream to the polls,” he said. “This is a fateful moment.”Voter sees election as ‘most important of all ones’“I think these elections are the most important of all the ones I’ve known,” said Ruth Epstein, an 81-year-old longtime left-wing voter in Ramat Gan near Tel Aviv, who voted for the opposition Democrats. “I’m really scared about what will be here.”Netanyahu has campaigned on an endorsement from US President Trump, his ally in war against Iran, who has said they should “finish the job”. If neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot can form a governing coalition in the 120-seat parliament, Netanyahu could stay on as caretaker until another election is held. His opponents have managed to wrest him from the premiership only once since 2009, and that took four inconclusive elections in two years. He was back 18 months later.Eisenkot sees ‘new spirit’For many of Netanyahu’s opponents, the election turns on accountability for the security failures of Oct 7. Opposition groups have promised to hold a national inquiry, which Netanyahu’s govt has resisted. “I am convinced that by the end of today, we will see a change — a new spirit for the State of Israel — that will serve as a rectification for the past three years and for that terrible day,” Eisenkot said.Eisenkot says Israel’s response was a failure because Hamas remains in charge. He repeated his commitment to dismantle or destroy Hamas’ military and governing power in Gaza within 18 months of forming a govt.Arab turnout a keyAhmed Tibi, a candidate from an Arab party, said the record turnout from Israel’s Arab minority would “pave the way for an alternative govt and change the grave reality”. Eisenkot has ruled out partnering with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values, although some possible scenarios envision them propping up a minority govt to topple Netanyahu. Netanyahu has repeatedly de­scribed Arab-Israeli voters as a threat in language his opponents say crosses into racism.Like nearly all Jewish party leaders in Israel, Eisenkot opposes the two-state solution that once underpinned decades of peace negotiations with the Palestinians. But he has criticised Jewish settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, which has surged since 2023 and strained Israel’s ties with Western states. articles.title: Manga artist Tetsuya Chiba, known for his boxing series ‘Ashita no Joe,’ passes away
articles.summary: Legendary Japanese manga artist Tetsuya Chiba, who caused a national sensation with his boxing series “Ashita no Joe” or “Fighting for Tomorrow,” a story
articles.body: Legendary Japanese manga artist Tetsuya Chiba, who caused a national sensation with his boxing series “Ashita no Joe” or “Fighting for Tomorrow,” a story about an orphan becoming a professional boxer, has died at 87. Chiba’s masterpiece series became so popular that fans even attended a mock funeral for the protagonist Joe Yabuki’s rival. Chiba died at a Tokyo hospital last Thursday, his publisher Kodansha Ltd. said Tuesday, without specifying the cause of his death.While he depicted aspiring young athletes fighting for their lives and careers, Chiba was a vocal supporter of peace and freedom of expression, telling stories of his harrowing memories of war as a child in autobiographical stories and manga. Months after he was born in Tokyo in Jan 1939, his family moved to China, and Chiba spent his early childhood there during Japan’s occupation in the region.At age 6, Chiba and his family marked Japan’s surrender on Aug 15, 1945, while they were still in China. There, they faced danger and hunger in the face of anti-Japanese riots, but survived. The family eventually fled to China’s port city of Huludao and returned to Japan in 1946.The memories later influenced his work and activity with an anti-war theme. Chiba debuted as a manga artist in 1956. In 1961, he debuted in a boys’ comic magazine with a baseball manga “Chikai no Makyu (The Magic Ball),” paving the way for a new genre of sports-themed manga in Japan.Chiba’s sports-themed manga also included “Ore wa Teppei (I’m Teppei),” the story of a high school student training in the martial art of kendo, “Notari Matsutaro”, about sumo wrestling, and “Ashita Tenki ni Naare (Let’s hope the weather’s fine tomorrow)”, about a teenage golfer.You use AI every day. articles.title: UK weather: Fog and mist to create dangerous driving conditions
articles.summary: After storms across the UK, the weather is set to turn calmer with mist and fog at times over the coming week.
articles.body:
Thick fog is forecast for parts of the UK this week, creating dangerous conditions for motorists, particularly around the morning commute.

Wednesday will be a day of some sunny spells and showers but as winds turn lighter into Thursday, extensive fog is expected to form.

The fog will lead to difficult driving conditions through the Thursday morning rush hour.

While rain is also in the forecast for the end of this week, as high pressure builds into November, more mist and fog will form next week.

After the recent stormy weather across the United Kingdom, things will turn calmer in the coming days.

The stormy spell of weather was caused by a very active jet stream - the fast moving wind high in the atmosphere - sending deep areas of low pressure toward the UK.

This is now going to weaken and instead of bringing low pressure systems, high pressure will start to develop.

High pressure brings more settled weather with lighter winds. In late autumn, it also brings the risk of mist, fog, low cloud, chillier days and frosty nights.

Wednesday will start off chillier compared to recent mornings and while dry for most, there will be lots of cloud and showery rain mainly across southern Scotland, northern England and north Wales.

This area of rain will move further south-east across Wales and into the Midlands during the morning before fading away.

The afternoon will then be largely dry with sunny spells across most areas of the UK with temperatures slightly above average at 12 to 16C.

During the night into Thursday, winds will lighten and mist and fog will develop, particularly in east Wales, central and southern England.

This could be dense in places and lead to some tricky driving conditions for the Thursday morning commute.

The fog may even linger in some parts until lunchtime.

By Friday and Saturday, some rain is likely across Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern areas of England and Wales.

But mist and fog may once again form across eastern and southern England.

High pressure will become more widely established over the weekend and into next week.

With light winds, more mist and fog is likely to form during the overnight periods and linger through the mornings.

In some places, the mist, fog and low cloud may not clear at all and make it feel quite chilly.

Much needed rain will also be in short supply.

Despite October giving the drought and severe drought areas of England and Wales around the average amount of October rainfall, some reservoirs are still exceptionally low .

This more settled weather pattern currently looks like it might continue for much of the first week of November.

articles.title: More than 100 people killed in Sudanese army drone attack on market, says Sudanese rights group
articles.summary: The strike, which the rights group says happened Monday evening, also injured 113 people.
articles.body: SHENDI, Sudan — More than 100 people were killed in a Sudanese military drone strike on a busy market in Nyala, the capital city of the South Darfur province in southwestern Sudan, said Emergency Lawyers, a rights group tracking violence in the country, in a statement Tuesday. The strike, which it says happened Monday evening, also injured 113 people. The group said many of those killed and injured were women and children. The group blamed the Sudanese military for the strike on the market, condemning the attack. “This massacre transformed a civilian marketplace into a scene of mass killing and injury and is an assault that threatens the lives of residents and compounds their suffering amid the ongoing war,” the group said in a statement. It called for an independent investigation into the strike. Doctors Without Borders, which is also known as Médecins Sans Frontières, or MSF, said earlier that 36 bodies arrived at its hospital in Nyala and reported seeing 150 injured in its emergency room. Nyala, the capital of South Darfur province, is controlled by the paramilitary group Rapid Support Forces, which has been fighting with the Sudanese army since 2023. Drone warfare has been a staple of the war, but in recent weeks, a massive escalation of drone strikes by both the RSF and the Sudanese army has killed hundreds. Both warring parties have increasingly launched explosive-laden drones that, in multiple cases, targeted civilian infrastructure, including hospitals, dams, schools, markets and displacement camps. Drone strikes have become the deadliest threat to civilians in this conflict, according to the U.N. The conflict has created the world’s largest humanitarian crisis, with about 34 million people — almost two out of every three Sudanese — needing assistance, according to the U.N. Sudan’s war started in April 2023 when tensions between the military and the RSF exploded into open fighting in the capital, Khartoum, and spread across the country. Previous strike leaves parts of Sudan without power Large parts of Sudan’s capital were without electricity for more than 12 hours Tuesday after a drone strike on a major power substation, according to an electric company official. The attack left hospitals and bakeries dependent on generators and limited water supplies across Khartoum. The state-run Sudanese Electricity Distribution Co. acknowledged “serious damage and technical faults” to the distribution network and several main stations and power lines but didn’t explain the reason in a statement. It apologized to residents across Khartoum state for repeated and prolonged outages. A company official, speaking to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the media, said a drone attack hit the Al-Markhiyat transformer station in Omdurman, on the outskirts of Khartoum. He said it is the second to hit the station this year, blaming it on the country’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. The RSF has been at war with the Sudanese military for more than three years. Sudan’s war began in April 2023, when simmering tensions between the military and the RSF exploded into open fighting in Khartoum and spread across the country. Deadly drone attacks across Sudan have been carried out by the two rival forces. But those attacks have become rare in Khartoum since the Sudanese military took control of the capital in May 2025, after years of brutal fighting between the military and the RSF. The U.N. has expressed concern over the use of drones across Sudan, saying they have been killing civilians, including children, and are disrupting essential services. The official who spoke to AP said technical teams are still assessing the damage, describing the strike as major. He estimated that 60% of the power supply in the capital could be affected, predicting that water stations will be most affected. A resident living near the Al-Markhiyat transformer station in Omdurman said he heard a drone shortly before the blast. “At around 4:30 in the morning, on my way to dawn prayers, I heard the sound of a drone very close by, and just moments later a huge explosion, and the power went out,” Abdel-Hafiz Abdel-Mutaal told AP. “I saw fire burning at the transformer station.” The city descended into darkness after sundown. Adel Ali, a resident of south Khartoum, said he was without power and water for 17 hours. “My main concern is how to preserve my insulin supply, which needs a fridge,” Ali, a diabetes patient, said. “Life without electricity is totally paralyzed, and a bread crisis is emerging as many bakeries have shut down.” He said this would drive the price of bread even higher. The electricity company, in its statement, said power rationing would be longer than usual in all areas until repairs are finished. It did not say when that would be. Technical teams were working around the clock to restore power, it added. The conflict has killed at least 59,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED, though aid groups say the true toll is likely higher. Over 67% of the country’s population is dependent on aid, while 825,000 children face acute malnutrition. The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, or IPC, a global food crisis monitor, warned last week that the “deteriorating humanitarian situation” across greater Darfur and Kordofan states is worsening, with food insecurity putting these areas at risk of famine. In a joint statement, over 30 countries, including the United States, United Kingdom and the European Commission, urged parties to the conflict in the country “to lift all impediments on humanitarian assistance.”

images.caption: A painting depicting people holding the Sudanese flag is seen on a wall damaged by bullets and shrapnel in Omdurman, on the outskirts of Khartoum, Sudan, Thursday, April 23, 2026.
